st.an: Leonard aligns closely with the cluster’s supervised-copilot framing: lawyers must verify generative-AI output, retain responsibility for work product and comply with existing duties of candor and supervision. Her discussion of unresolved billing effects and unequal adoption resources also supports the cluster’s view that commercial gains depend on organizational context and remain unsettled.
qs: It reminds lawyers not to uncritically rely on GenAI-generated content, especially in litigation, and to double-check everything for accuracy before filing anything or citing case law.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty

kp.k: Ethics opinions guide practice without constituting binding precedent
kp.d: McCormack distinguishes bar ethics opinions from legislation and substantive court decisions. She says the opinions are not binding precedent and departure from their advice does not automatically establish liability, but courts and regulators often treat them as authoritative statements of professional norms. The speakers recommend using the ABA and relevant state guidance to plan AI adoption.
qs: Now, none of these ethics opinions are binding precedent in any way.
But these opinions are often relied on by courts and regulators as authoritative sources of the norms and best practices in the profession.

kp.k: Existing ethical duties require new technological understanding
kp.d: Leonard describes ABA Formal Opinion 512, issued earlier in 2024, as a 15-page treatment of existing professional obligations rather than a rewriting of them. In her account, competence requires understanding AI capabilities and limitations, not expertise in the underlying technology. McCormack agrees that lawyers need enough technological knowledge to discharge unchanged duties to clients, adversaries, tribunals and the public.
qs: I think notably, it says that lawyers do not need to become experts in the underlying technology, but they should generally be familiar with what the tools can and cannot do.
You might have to make sure you understand enough about the technology to be able to carry out those duties that you swore an oath to uphold—but the duties themselves don’t change.

kp.k: Confidentiality and client disclosure constrain AI deployment
kp.d: Leonard identifies safeguarding client information as a major law-firm concern. In summarizing Opinion 512, she cautions against entering confidential or sensitive information into public models and identifies hypothetical questions used for client work as an unresolved area. She reports commentary emphasizing client disclosure when AI is central to strategy or substantive work, rather than asserting a universal disclosure requirement for every use.
qs: So, being sure you understand whether you’re using a public model, where you should be putting in no confidential or sensitive information at all.

Most of the commentary I’ve seen has focused on the client communication part—this idea that if you’re using GenAI in a way that’s central to your engagement, especially for strategy or substantive work, the client needs to know.

kp.k: Human verification and supervision remain lawyers’ responsibilities
kp.d: Leonard links the opinion’s emphasis on candor to incidents involving fabricated citations. Her account stresses accuracy checks before court filings or citation of cases and continued lawyer responsibility for AI-produced work. This is a professional-duty argument prompted by sanctions incidents, not evidence of measured model error rates.
qs: It reminds lawyers not to uncritically rely on GenAI-generated content, especially in litigation, and to double-check everything for accuracy before filing anything or citing case law.
Lawyers remain responsible for the work product that comes out of generative AI.

kp.k: Pennsylvania guidance raises contested programmer liability questions
kp.d: McCormack paraphrases Pennsylvania’s ethics opinion as suggesting that nonlawyer AI programmers may violate the state’s Rule 5.5 and that legal advice or judgment requires licensed-attorney involvement. Both speakers interpret the language as potentially reaching frontier-model developers whose products consumers use for legal help, but doubt that this will be its practical effect. Their discussion presents unresolved interpretations and enforcement concerns, not a finding that developers have committed unauthorized practice.
qs: To the extent that the AI programmer is not a lawyer, the programmer may violate Rule 5.5 regarding the unauthorized practice of law.
I think this section leaves room for different interpretations.

It does feel hard for me to believe that’s what it’s going to mean in practice, because I am sure—in fact I’m already aware—of people in Pennsylvania who are not lawyers who have used the technology to get help with legal problems.

kp.k: Consumer self-help complicates restrictive unauthorized-practice approaches
kp.d: McCormack recounts a Pennsylvania tenant using ChatGPT information to negotiate with her landlord about a leaky roof when she lacked other options. This anecdote grounds her skepticism about criminal enforcement against model engineers. Leonard predicts that a restrictive codification would create an impractical volume of enforcement targets; neither offers systematic evidence of consumer outcomes or safety.
qs: And she was able to get some help and information from ChatGPT and use it to negotiate with her landlord.
Was Sam Altman or his engineering team guilty of a felony in that case? I find it very hard to believe.
One is, I think the state Supreme Court would be engaged in a game of whack-a-mole the likes of which we’ve never seen, trying to identify everyone in the Commonwealth using these technologies.

kp.k: Minnesota sandbox targets unmet civil legal needs
kp.d: McCormack reports that the Minnesota state bar approved a committee to establish a generative-AI regulatory sandbox focused on access to justice. She describes a prospective supervised environment for technologists, lawyers and others to explore services despite regulatory barriers, especially UPL, while monitoring consumer harm. She qualifies its novelty as the first generative-AI-focused sandbox she knows of; potential breakthroughs are aspirations, not demonstrated results.
qs: But the state bar greenlighted a new committee that's going to stand up a generative AI regulatory sandbox tasked with improving access to justice.
Most people can't afford legal help with their civil justice problems. And so they either just try and manage on their own, or they give up.

So the sandbox is a way to leverage the technology to help people, and give the technologists, lawyers, others who want to explore these options a safe place to do it, where the bar can also monitor the use of the technology in the sandbox to make sure that consumers are not harmed.

kp.k: Efficiency may become an ethical expectation in billing
kp.d: McCormack reads Minnesota’s fee discussion as suggesting that lawyers probably have an ethical obligation to use AI where it makes tasks significantly more efficient. She supports this interpretation with language quoted from another ethics opinion about not charging for time caused by inexperience. Her claim is conditional on available efficiency gains, rather than a categorical mandate to use AI for all work.
qs: Minnesota reminds lawyers about the other side of that—that if lawyers could be using the technology to do certain tasks significantly more efficiently, they probably have an ethical obligation to do it.
Lawyers must remember that they may not charge clients for time necessitated by their own inexperience.

So yes, learn what you need to learn to use the technology to help your clients, because otherwise, if you're charging them to do tasks manually that you could be doing far more efficiently, they may have a reason to complain about your service.

kp.k: Time savings challenge hourly pricing and cost allocation
kp.d: Leonard reports that the ABA opinion’s fee discussion raises questions about billing for dramatically faster work and passing technology costs to clients. She describes concern that substantial task-time reductions could undermine the billable-hour model. Later, she reports firms learning from immigration partners’ longstanding flat-fee experience as a possible guide to changing pricing, without claiming an observed profession-wide transition.
qs: There’s also a real concern about the business model—if GenAI fundamentally changes how long things take, then the billable hour model might not make sense anymore, and that’s a big shift.
Because immigration is a service that lawyers provide that has been a flat-fee service for a very long time.
And so those lawyers are really well positioned to provide guidance to the rest of the profession, I think, as we think through the way that we charge for our services.

kp.k: Smaller practices face unequal short-term adoption burdens
kp.d: Both speakers identify learning time, training expense and tool acquisition as obstacles for small and midsize firms and solos. Leonard bases this on what she hears from practices and worries that global firms can adapt faster because of greater resources. She predicts long-term benefits for smaller practices while expressing concern about insufficient support during the transition; the transcript supplies no comparative adoption data.
qs: It's like, A, they don't have the time, because at any level of your practice in any one of those models, you just don't have the time to build in these things—the learning process.
But also, the investment you would need to make in having somebody come in and teach you how to use this, or in acquiring the tools themselves—I think that they're really grappling in the short term.
And I am worried that we're not being supportive enough of everybody else who serves a lot of different parts of the legal marketplace.

kp.k: Workshops encourage redesign beyond automating existing tasks
kp.d: Leonard describes workshops using public frontier models with anonymized hypothetical situations to broaden lawyers’ thinking beyond leases, briefs and research tools. McCormack contrasts inserting AI into existing workflows with reimagining whole problems or workstreams, which she considers more consequential. Leonard’s participant anecdotes suggest possibilities for improved RFPs, anticipating general counsel needs and identifying new services, rather than measured business growth.
qs: And so a lot of those workshops involve lawyers sitting down in a room together with their laptops, using a public frontier model and an anonymized hypothetical situation.
how do we just reimagine this entire workstream or this entire problem that we're trying to solve now that we have these new tools?

Well, it also surfaced this thing that we don't currently offer through this practice group. But if we had time, we might be able to build this out as a service that's really in need, but nobody has this yet.

kp.k: Expert judgment and iterative prompting support practical augmentation
kp.d: Leonard describes using AI to generate workshop ideas and draft and critique instructions, with her expertise filtering useful suggestions. McCormack recommends asking models how to obtain desired responses and explains prompting through context, examples, limits and follow-up questions. These are personal practice recommendations and qualitative efficiency observations, not controlled productivity findings.
qs: And I'll think, okay, you know, four of those are really good ideas; the other six are gonna be eye rolls from law firm partners.
But that's how it works really well right now—when you can apply your expertise

Setting limits is helpful. Giving the model examples of the kind of thing you're looking for is helpful. And then the follow-up questions you ask are sometimes almost as important as the original ones.

kp.k: Customized GPTs offer internal information-access applications
kp.d: McCormack reports American Arbitration Association personnel building customized GPTs across internal data as a step toward chatbots for HR information and internal policies. She presents consolidation of information dispersed across the website and SharePoint as a practical benefit. This is an organizational use example rather than evidence of legal-role substitution or quantified savings.
qs: we have a number of people building them across our internal data at the American Arbitration Association, which is quite useful.
And it's sort of a step along the way to building some chatbots, which will be useful for everybody for things like HR information and other internal policies and practices.
So building all of the information around one topic into a GPT has been one helpful way to interact with that information.

kp.k: Rapid guidance signals change but requires continuing revision
kp.d: McCormack praises acknowledgment that ethics opinions may need regular updating as AI changes. Leonard interprets the speed of AI guidance, contrasted with ABA opinions on reply-all in 2022 and listserv usage earlier in 2024, as a signal that professional bodies expect significant practice changes. The speakers view guidance as useful for initiating adoption discussions even if it soon becomes outdated.
qs: One thing I particularly appreciate—both in the ABA opinion and in some state opinions—is the acknowledgement that because the technology is changing so quickly, the opinions themselves may need to be updated regularly.

I think—even if the opinions are outdated six months from now because the technology has already moved so quickly that there are new considerations—they’ve been useful in starting these conversations.
But I think the signal that all of these opinions are sending is: this technology’s here, and we think that it will seriously change the way that lawyers practice.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The speakers describe current augmentation of legal and organisational work, predict changes to pricing and competitive conditions, and identify both ethical constraints and potential access-to-justice benefits.
pts.d: Jen Leonard reports that AI helps her develop workshop guides, identify confusing instructions and generate business-development ideas, particularly when she applies professional expertise to select and refine outputs. Her workshop accounts suggest potential for faster RFP preparation and identifying additional client services, rather than establishing measured commercial results. Bridget McCormack argues that redesigning entire workflows offers greater impact than inserting AI into existing processes. She also reports useful internal GPT development at the American Arbitration Association. Leonard predicts that substantial time savings could undermine hourly billing and that AI will be a long-term 'game changer' for smaller practices, while warning that larger firms may adopt faster because of superior resources. McCormack interprets Minnesota's fees guidance as implying a probable ethical obligation to use AI when it makes tasks significantly more efficient. Both speakers maintain that AI changes how lawyers discharge existing duties, not the duties themselves: human supervision, verification and responsibility remain necessary. They question whether Pennsylvania's UPL approach could implicate frontier-model developers when nonlawyers obtain legal help directly; Leonard predicts severe enforcement difficulties if that interpretation were codified. McCormack presents Minnesota's proposed AI sandbox as a possible route to new access-to-justice solutions, not as evidence of demonstrated outcomes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists primarily of personal use, workshop observations, practitioner feedback and the speakers' interpretations of ethics opinions; no quantitative productivity or market evidence is supplied.
pts.d: Leonard grounds her augmentation claims in her own workshop-design work and feedback from participating lawyers. Reported participant reactions illustrate possibilities, not independently demonstrated revenue gains or time savings. Her account of smaller firms' constraints draws on conversations with those practices. McCormack grounds the internal-information claim in GPT projects at the AAA and illustrates direct public use with an anecdote about her child's friend using ChatGPT in a landlord negotiation. Neither anecdote establishes general reliability or outcomes across users. The ethical claims rely on discussion of ABA Formal Opinion 512 and Pennsylvania and Minnesota bar opinions, rather than independent analysis of the underlying documents supplied here. Fabricated-citation incidents are invoked as background for verification and candor duties, not as measured hallucination rates. Minnesota's committee and proposed sandbox provide an institutional basis for discussing experimentation, but the transcript reports no sandbox results. Predictions about billing, long-term competitive effects, enforcement impracticality and access-to-justice breakthroughs are the speakers' judgments.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current benefits are conditional on expert use and oversight; competitive gains and regulatory implications remain prospective and uncertain.
pts.d: In this 2024 discussion, workshop assistance and AAA internal GPT work are described as current activities. Leonard explicitly conditions effective use on applying expertise; her workshops use public models with anonymized hypotheticals. Faster RFP work, additional services and improved leisure time are possibilities rather than guaranteed outcomes, and she warns against filling saved time with more work. She distinguishes short-term learning and investment difficulties for smaller firms from anticipated long-term benefits, without giving a date or quantified forecast. Potential hourly-billing disruption depends on AI materially reducing task duration. McCormack's efficiency-based ethical obligation is qualified as probable and applies to tasks that could be performed significantly more efficiently. Both speakers describe ethics opinions as nonbinding guidance that may influence courts and regulators, with possible rapid revision as technology changes. The Pennsylvania concerns are conditional interpretations and hypothetical consequences of future codification, not reports of established liability. Minnesota's sandbox is described as forthcoming, with consumer monitoring integral to its proposed experimentation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern practising lawyers, differently resourced firms, clients, legal-service organisations, underserved individuals, technology developers and professional regulators.
pts.d: Lawyers and practice groups may gain faster drafting and business-development support, new service ideas and potentially more personal time, but retain responsibility for verifying AI output and protecting clients. AAA staff may gain easier access to dispersed internal policies. Small and midsize firms and solo practices face limited learning time and investment capacity; Leonard anticipates longer-term benefits for small, solo and plaintiff-side practices while expressly excluding contingency plaintiff-side practices from that particular statement. Large global firms are portrayed as better resourced for early adoption. Clients could receive more efficient service and have grounds to question charges for avoidably manual work. Leonard suggests that immigration practitioners' longstanding flat-fee experience could guide other lawyers reconsidering pricing. Individuals unable to afford civil legal help are the intended beneficiaries of the Minnesota sandbox and the population illustrated by McCormack's landlord-negotiation anecdote. Frontier-model programmers and companies could face UPL questions under the speakers' reading of Pennsylvania's opinion, while courts and bars would confront enforcement and consumer-protection challenges. These public access claims are distinct from enterprise cost savings.
